title: Add method Elements.before(Node node)

judge.reasoning:
Both patches add `Elements.before(Node)` and `after(Node)`, and both resolve the issue. They differ in what happens to the supplied node.

Patch A follows jQuery's model. Each target except the last gets a deep clone, and the last target gets the original node, which is moved. The clones are all made before any insertion, so they don't capture earlier insertions into the node's own subtree. A test (`beforeNodeContainingMatches`) covers this case.

Patch B clones for every target and leaves the original untouched. That matches the user's `outerHtml()` workaround, so it is also reasonable. However, B makes each clone lazily inside the loop. If the supplied node contains any of the matched elements, earlier insertions change the node before it is cloned again, and later copies include those earlier clones. B neither handles nor tests this.

Placement: A puts the logic in `Nodes`, alongside the existing `Nodes.before(String)` and `after(String)`, and adds covariant overrides in `Elements`. This follows the existing class split and also gives the feature to `Nodes<TextNode>` and similar collections. B adds the methods only to `Elements`.

Tests: A's are stronger. They cover identity of the original versus the clones, a single-element chain, the self-containing case, and the `Nodes` variants. B tests output and that the original keeps a null parent.

Scope: B also adds `prepend(Node)` and `append(Node)`. That is beyond the ask, so it is neutral. B also removes the `Iterator` and `Predicate` imports from `Elements.java`. That is unrelated churn, and if either import is still used it breaks compilation.

Overall, A is more complete, better structured, better tested and lower risk.

title: XML parser does not support DOCTYPE with <!ENTITY> declarations

judge.reasoning: The issue is about `Jsoup.clean()`. `clean()` parses its input with the HTML body-fragment parser, not the XML parser. Patch A changes the doctype tokeniser states for every syntax and adds a `DoctypeInternalSubset` state. That state skips quoted strings, comments, PIs and markup declarations, then hands the trailing `]...>` to BogusDoctype. As a result, the `]>` and the entity declarations no longer leak as text in the HTML or the XML parser. Patch A's CleanerTest reproduces the issue's exact `Jsoup.clean` scenario, and HtmlParserTest checks `parseBodyFragment`. It also covers many doctype variants (`svg[`, `SYSTEM[`, `PUBLIC`, quoted `]>`), protects against a stray `[` swallowing the document, and handles EOF. Patch B gates every new transition on `t.syntax == xml`. The HTML tokeniser path used by `Jsoup.clean()` is therefore unchanged, and the reported `]>` artifact would most likely still appear. B's own test shows that HTML output simply drops the subset after the doctype; it never exercises `clean()`. B adds a reasonable XML round-trip feature (keeping the subset in `DocumentType`), but that does not address the reported scenario. B also lacks A's guard: an unterminated subset consumes the whole rest of the document, a behaviour B's test asserts as intended. A's change to HTML tokenisation departs slightly from the spec's bogus-doctype handling, but it is well contained and tested. Patch A fixes the actual bug; Patch B likely does not.

issue_md:
When `Jsoup.clean()` processes XML/SVG input that contains a DOCTYPE declaration with an internal DTD subset (i.e., entity declarations enclosed in `[...]`), jsoup correctly removes the DOCTYPE tag itself but leaves the closing ]> of the subset in the output string.

This was discovered while sanitizing SVG files that follow the Adobe Illustrator export format.

jsoup version: *1.22.1*
Java version: 25

## Steps to Reproduce

Call Jsoup.clean() with the following input SVG that contains a DOCTYPE with multiple <!ENTITY> declarations inside an internal DTD subset:

```
import org.jsoup.Jsoup;
import org.jsoup.nodes.Document;
import org.jsoup.safety.Safelist;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

class SvgSanitizerTest {
    Safelist safelist = Safelist.none()
            .addTags("svg", "circle")
            .addAttributes("svg", "viewBox")
            .addAttributes("circle", "cx", "cy", "r", "fill");


    @Test
    void shouldRemoveDocTypeTag() {
        String dirtySvg = """
                <?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
                <!DOCTYPE svg PUBLIC "-//W3C//DTD SVG 1.1//EN" "http://www.w3.org/Graphics/SVG/1.1/DTD/svg11.dtd" [
                	<!ENTITY ns_extend "http://ns.adobe.com/Extensibility/1.0/">
                	<!ENTITY ns_ai "http://ns.adobe.com/AdobeIllustrator/10.0/">
                	<!ENTITY ns_graphs "http://ns.adobe.com/Graphs/1.0/">
                	<!ENTITY ns_vars "http://ns.adobe.com/Variables/1.0/">
                	<!ENTITY ns_imrep "http://ns.adobe.com/ImageReplacement/1.0/">
                	<!ENTITY ns_sfw "http://ns.adobe.com/SaveForWeb/1.0/">
                	<!ENTITY ns_custom "http://ns.adobe.com/GenericCustomNamespace/1.0/">
                	<!ENTITY ns_adobe_xpath "http://ns.adobe.com/XPath/1.0/">
                ]>
                <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 100 100">
                  <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="red"/>
                </svg>
                """;
        String expectedSvg = """
                <svg viewBox="0 0 100 100">
                      <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="red" />
                  </svg>
                """;

        Document.OutputSettings outputSettings = new Document.OutputSettings()
                .syntax(Document.OutputSettings.Syntax.xml)
                .prettyPrint(false);

        var cleanedSvg = Jsoup.clean(dirtySvg, "", safelist, outputSettings);

        assertThat(cleanedSvg).isEqualToNormalizingWhitespace(expectedSvg);
    }

}

```

## Expected Behaviour
The entire DOCTYPE block (including its internal subset [...]>) is removed. Output:
```
<svg viewBox="0 0 100 100">
  <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="red" />
</svg>
```

## Actual Behaviour
The DOCTYPE declaration is removed but the closing ]> of the internal DTD subset is left behind in the output:
```
]>
<svg viewBox="0 0 100 100">
  <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="red" />
</svg>
```
## Impact
Any application using Jsoup.clean() to sanitize SVG (or XML) produced by tools like Adobe Illustrator will silently receive malformed output containing the ]> artifact, which can break downstream XML parsers and SVG renderers.

Could you please have a look into this please ?
Kindly let me know if you need any more details about the issue.
Many thanks in advance!!

BR
Ram

title: Align parser scope classification with HTML spec

judge.reasoning:
Both patches make the same changes to the scope lists: they add `select` to TagsSearchInScope and `template` to TagSearchTableScope, keeping both arrays sorted. The difference is in the SVG special-element fix.

Patch B checks the normalized name against TagSearchInScopeSvg, the existing lowercase list (`desc`, `foreignobject`, `title`). This removes the case mismatch at its root and works however the element was built or which ParseSettings were used.

Patch A instead compares the case-preserved `tagName()` against TagSvgHtmlIntegration using an unsorted linear `in`. That works when the parser has case-adjusted the name to `foreignObject`. It fails for an SVG element whose tagName is lowercase `foreignobject`, which can happen through programmatic construction or other settings. Patch A also switches away from the `inSorted` normalized-name convention the rest of `isSpecial` uses.

On tests, Patch A adds only two membership assertions, which are close to tautological, and one `isSpecial` check on a parsed foreignObject. It also deletes three imports with no explanation. Patch B adds behavioral tests that would fail before the fix and pass after it:
- `li` and `dd` inside foreignObject stay contained.
- A stray `</x-a>` stops at foreignObject.
- A stray `</tr>` inside a template in a cell does not escape the template.
- Direct `inScope` and `inTableScope` checks on a constructed stack confirm the boundary semantics, including that `select` does not affect table scope.

Patch B's changelog entry is also more informative. Overall, B is more robust and much better tested.

issue_md:
I saw that jsoup's HTML tree-builder classification lists are missing a few entries from the current WHATWG HTML parsing spec: `select` is not included as an ordinary in-scope boundary, `template` is not included as a table-scope boundary, and SVG `foreignObject` is not treated as a special element (because the special element check compares the normalized name (`foreignobject`) with the case-preserved integration-point name (`foreignObject`))

Spec references:

- Has an element in scope: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/parsing.html#has-an-element-in-scope
- Has an element in table scope: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/parsing.html#has-an-element-in-table-scope
- Special elements: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/parsing.html#special

title: Mixed-case RCDATA end tags can promote text to markup

judge.reasoning: Both patches fix the root cause the same way. Each replaces the lower-case/upper-case `nextIndexOf` probes in `containsIgnoreCase` with a linear case-insensitive scan of the buffer, so mixed-case closers like `` are now found. Both keep the scan cache consistent: Patch A stores `bufPos + offset` after `bufferUp`, and Patch B stores the absolute index after calling `bufferUp` up front. Correctness is effectively equal. Tests are comparable. Both replace the old `assertFalse("one")` with a positive assertion and add a mixed-case `CharacterReader` test. Both add parser-level tests for the issue's `<p>` and `<textarea>` cases that would fail before the change. A's parser test checks a little more (the following `<p>Bar</p>` and `textarea.val()`), and B's checks that no `fake` or `body p` element is created. Neither is meaningfully weaker. The difference is in craft. Patch B extracts `rangeMatchesIgnoreCase` from the existing `matchesIgnoreCase`, so the new scan reuses the comparison logic already in the class rather than duplicating it. Patch A adds a separate `charsEqualIgnoreCase` helper and a new `nextIndexOfIgnoreCase` method. That is a parallel implementation of the same comparison, with slightly different semantics (an extra lower-case-of-upper check), which adds a second place to maintain. B also calls `bufferUp()` before the cache check, which makes the cached-index comparison against `bufPos` more obviously sound. B adds a CHANGES entry, which is neutral-to-positive. On balance B is the slightly cleaner, more cohesive fix.

issue_md:
RCDATA elements like `` and `<textarea>` should match their end tags case-insensitively. A direct mixed-case closer works as expected: `<title>Foo` closes the title. But when tag-shaped text appears before the closer, jsoup can miss the mixed-case end tag and leave RCDATA early. For example, `<p>Foo` creates a real `body p` element instead of keeping `

Foo` as title text. Similarly, `` creates an `img` element. This was a premature optimization: the implementation only looked for consistent-case matches. I’ll fix it with a real case-insensitive scan.

title: W3CDom serializes plain XML with the reserved XML namespace
issue_md:
Plain XML parsed with `Parser.xmlParser()` should round-trip through the default namespace-aware `W3CDom` conversion as parseable XML. But for an ordinary no-namespace XML document, `W3CDom` currently serializes jsoup's internal XML parser namespace as the document's default namespace.

For example, converting `<root><child>One</child></root>` through `new W3CDom().fromJsoup(doc)` and `W3CDom.asString(..., W3CDom.OutputXml())` emits `<root xmlns="http://www.w3.org/XML/1998/namespace">...`. That namespace is reserved for the `xml` prefix and cannot be bound as the default namespace, so a normal XML parser rejects the output.

Fix is to keep explicit source namespaces as W3C DOM namespaces, but map our internal plain-XML sentinel namespace to no namespace when creating unprefixed W3C elements. `xml:*` attributes such as `xml:lang` should continue to use the reserved XML namespace.

title: Review HttpClient's thread use under heavy request load

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the root cause the same way: requests with no authenticator and no custom SSLContext now share one static HttpClient instead of each Connection building its own client with its own selector and worker threads. Both also rebuild the shared client when the JVM default SSLContext changes.

Patch A goes further with a weakly keyed pool of shared clients per custom SSLContext. That extra machinery (WeakHashMap plus WeakReference values) is beyond the issue's ask and adds some subtlety: clients can be collected and rebuilt. Patch A also keeps the old unsynchronized per-connection logic for the authenticator path. Its standout test is an integration test that counts SelectorManager threads across repeated `Jsoup.connect` calls, which directly measures the reported symptom.

Patch B introduces an immutable ClientState holding (client, authenticator, sslContext) with a single `matches` check. It uses double-checked locking for both the shared client and the per-connection client, so concurrent requests on a session can't race to create duplicate clients. It replaces the two loosely coupled fields (`client`, `lastAuth`) with one volatile state field, which is clearer and fixes a latent ordering quirk in the old reuse logic. Its tests check:
- sharing across connections
- that concurrent lazy initialization yields a single client
- default-SSL refresh
- rebuilds when the authenticator or SSL context changes
- an integration test that mixed proxied and direct concurrent requests through the now-shared client keep proxy routes isolated

That last test covers the main new risk of sharing a client, since proxy settings are per-request thread-locals. Patch B's test refactor to @AfterEach is minor churn but harmless.

Overall, both are correct. Patch B's design is more robust under the concurrent heavy-load scenario the issue describes, and its tests better cover the correctness risks introduced by sharing. Patch A has the nicer direct thread-count test but more complex pooling and no concurrency hardening.

issue_md:
#2515 reports that many repeated requests will spawn many threads, probably redundant. They do get reaped on GC pressure, but there is likely to be better ways to reuse them via a keep-alive pool or similar.

@rs1gg thanks for raising this!

title: Element.html(Appendable) violates the contract of Node.html(Appendable)

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the issue the same way: they make `Node#outerHtml(Appendable)` public so an element's outer HTML can be streamed. Both also document that `Element#html(Appendable)` writes inner HTML, consistent with `html()`. Both handle `Document` so it writes no wrapper tag.

Patch A does this with the smallest possible change. It widens the visibility from protected to public and keeps the `void` signature, which is binary- and source-compatible. It adds a `Document` override that delegates to `html(accum)`. Its tests check the result against `outerHtml()` and `html()`, cover non-element nodes and building a fragment from several elements, and run from outside the `org.jsoup.nodes` package to show the method is now public.

Patch B changes the signature to a generic `<T extends Appendable> T outerHtml(T)`. That breaks binary compatibility, so it has to add a japicmp exclusion in `pom.xml` and argue that no downstream code overrides the method. It also removes `Document#outerHtml()` (String) and instead overrides `outerHtml(QuietAppendable)`. That drops the old `super.html()` path, which trimmed output under pretty-print, so `Document.outerHtml()` may now behave differently. It also refactors `Element#html` into a package-private `QuietAppendable` overload. The return value for chaining is a nicer API, and its tests are also solid, including `assertSame` and prefix checks. But the extra signature changes, the build-config exclusion and the altered `Document.outerHtml()` path add risk without being needed to fix the issue.

On correctness and tests the two are about equal, and A's scope is tighter and lower-risk, so A wins.

issue_md:
The contract of `Node.html(Appendable)` states: "Write **this node** and its children to the given Appendable", but if you call Element.html(Appendable) only the children of the Element are appended:

https://github.com/jhy/jsoup/blob/d8c49e5ec72a08ca1ac4e08740e70dc0f47ad911/src/main/java/org/jsoup/nodes/Element.java#L2047

On the other hand, `Node.outerHtml(Appendable)` is `protected`, and the class `Printer` is not visible too.

It would be very useful to have a method to write all the HTML of an element and its content, especially when one have to generate HTML fragments. The `String outerHtml()` method is `public` and does the job, but it's obvious that the version that accept an Appendable is more efficient if the caller has an Appendable ready to use.

title: Parse CDATA as a bogus comment in HTML content

judge.reasoning:
Both patches correctly make `<![CDATA[` in HTML-namespace content a bogus comment that ends at the next `>`. Both keep CDATA in SVG, MathML and the XML parser.

The difference is in fragment parsing, where the spec's 'adjusted current node' is the context element.

Patch A keeps the real context tag, including its namespace, when it builds the fragment context element. Fragments parsed inside `<svg>` or `<math>` therefore behave as foreign content all the way down: nested children get the SVG/MathML namespace, and CDATA inside those nested children is still recognized. It also fixes the knock-on effects of keeping the namespace:
- tokeniser start state only switches to script, plaintext or template mode for HTML contexts;
- noscript handling only applies to HTML contexts;
- `resetInsertionMode` treats non-HTML nodes without `continue`, which also removes a latent null dereference.
These changes are broader, but each follows from honouring the context namespace and is covered by tests (SVG and MathML fragments, HTML integration points, foreign script/plaintext/noscript contexts, custom foreign data tags).

Patch B adds a side field, `contextNamespace`, and consults it only while the context element is the sole item on the stack. The context copy itself stays in the HTML namespace. As a result, `svg.html("<g><![CDATA[x]]></g>")` would create an HTML-namespace `<g>`, and the CDATA inside it would wrongly become a bogus comment. Its fix is partial for fragments.

Patch B's tokenizer change (`matches && allowsCdata && matchConsume`, falling through to the existing bogus-comment branch) and its virtual `allowsCdata` in `TreeBuilder` are tidy.

On tests, both update the existing CDATA tests and add HTML-vs-foreign cases. Patch A's tests are more thorough: integration points, nested SVG, XML with the HTML namespace, error position, and fragment namespaces.

Patch A wins on correctness and test depth.

issue_md:
The HTML parser currently recognizes `<![CDATA[...]]>` in all contexts and creates a `CDataNode`.

Per the HTML specification, CDATA sections are recognized only in foreign content such as SVG and MathML.

In the HTML namespace, `<![CDATA[` is a parse error and should start a bogus comment, which ends at the next `>`.

Update the tokenizer to consider the adjusted current node’s namespace so that HTML parsing aligns with browser behavior.

CDATA handling should remain unchanged for SVG, MathML, and XML parsing.

title: Correct offsite link detection in Cleaner
issue_md:
The Cleaner uses a string-prefix comparison to determine whether a link points to the same site as the document base URI.

This can incorrectly treat a prefixed hostname as local when the base URI has no trailing slash, and can treat local links as external when the base URI contains a path.

Parse and compare the resolved link and base URI hostnames instead.

Relative links should remain local, while absolute links should be considered external when no base URI is available.

title: Normalize re2j exceptions

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the root cause the issue describes. Before either change, only re2j compile was guarded; a StackOverflowError raised during re2j matching (Matcher.find, which is where re2j#77's recursion occurs) escaped as a raw Error. Both patches wrap Re2jRegex's find() and rethrow a ValidationException, so on correctness for the reported re2j case they are equivalent.

Patch A also adds the same handling to the JDK regex path, in both compile and find. That is extra hardening beyond the issue's re2j ask, so it earns no credit on its own. It is mostly harmless, but it widens the behavior change to every jsoup user, not just re2j users.

On craft, Patch A keeps the `"Pattern complexity error: " + e.getMessage()` form. StackOverflowError usually has a null message, so users will typically see "Pattern complexity error: null". Patch B emits a clean "Pattern complexity error" message via a named constant, which matches the issue's wording exactly.

On tests, Patch B adds a focused regression test that reproduces the real-world scenario: a selector query (`[data-key~=(a|){824}]`) run through doc.select with re2j enabled. It asserts the exact normalized message, and it would fail before the change with a raw StackOverflowError. Patch A's tests are broader but weaker in two ways. Its re2j compile test exercises a path that was already guarded before the patch, so it would pass without the fix. Its other tests depend on 100k-deep inputs and default stack sizes, which makes them heavier and potentially environment-sensitive, though its re2j find test is a valid regression test.

Overall, B delivers the issue's fix more cleanly and precisely, with a tighter targeted test. A adds broader but unrequested scope and produces a sloppy 'null'-suffixed message.

issue_md:
re2j can throw a Stack Overflow if the input regex causes a deep recursion. We should normalize that into an `Pattern complexity error` ValidationException (which is an IllegalArgumentException) so it's clearer what the issue is.

Underlying root cause is https://github.com/google/re2j/issues/77

title: Element.appendChild allows self-parenting and creates a cyclic DOM tree

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the reported `e.appendChild(e)` case. Each adds a check that rejects inserting a node that is the target itself or one of its ancestors, with the same fast exit for childless nodes. Both check every child before moving any, so a rejected batch leaves the tree unchanged.

Patch A puts the check inside `setParentNode`, so it covers any path that reparents a node. To do that it restructures `addChildren`, `replaceChild` and the in-place fast path around a new `setParentNodeUnchecked`. That is broader, but it is more churn in hot code, and it changes the fast path, which now goes through `removeChild` logic it skipped before.

Patch A also misses one case. When a detached node calls `replaceWith(in)`, it borrows `in`'s parent before any check runs. If `in` is a descendant of that node, the node's parent pointer is already set to its own descendant. That is a parent cycle, and it can stay in place when the operation then fails.

Patch B checks at each entry point: `appendChild`, `before`/`after`, `replaceChild`, both `addChildren` overloads, and explicitly that detached `replaceWith` case, before any mutation. It is a smaller, less risky change to the existing code. It also moves `noNullElements` ahead of the fast path, which is a small robustness gain.

On tests, both suites would fail before the fix and pass after. Patch B's suite is broader: self and ancestor checks for append, prepend, insert, `appendTo`, `before`/`after`, `replaceWith`, the fast path, the detached-replace case, and a check that legitimate same-parent moves still work. Patch A tests atomic batch rejection and moving a populated subtree, both useful, but not `before`/`after` or the detached case.

Patch A's CHANGES entry is a minor plus. Overall, Patch B covers more edge cases with less risk and better tests.

title: W3CDom throws NPE for element names with invalid XML starts

judge.reasoning:
Patch B is the better fix: both resolve the reported NPE, but A widens the change into attribute handling without testing it, while B keeps the fix confined to tag names.

**Correctness.**
- Both patches stop the NPE by normalizing `1abc` to `_1abc` when the name cannot start an XML name.
- Patch A puts the fallback inside the shared `w3cSafeName` and deletes the `if (key == null) return;` guard in `setAttribute`. Attributes that were previously skipped as unrepresentable are now emitted with a `_` prefix, or as a bare `_` as the last resort.
- That contradicts the existing changelog note that unrepresentable attributes are skipped. It also allows several attributes to collapse to the same `_` key, or to collide with declaration handling.
- None of this attribute-path change is tested.
- Patch B fixes the root helper `Normalizer.xmlSafeTagName`, which is the shared tag-name normalizer, and applies it before QName normalization for element names only. Attribute behavior is unchanged.
- B also fixes the same root cause in `Element.safeTagName`, where XML-syntax serialization previously emitted `<null>`. That is a closely related symptom of the same null return, and it carries little risk.

**Tests.**
- Patch A tests `1abc` and `-abc` with a nested child and checks parentage.
- Patch B tests a renamed root (`1abc`), a prefixed name with an invalid local part (`p:2x` → `p:_2x`), and text content and serialized output.
- B also covers a programmatically created element (`9lives`) in an HTML document, matching both scenarios in the issue (created and renamed elements).
- B adds an `ElementTest` showing XML serialization is fixed while HTML syntax is unchanged.
- B's tests are broader and exercise the prefix case.

**Scope and craft.**
- Patch A's CHANGES entry is a plus, but its silent change to attribute semantics adds risk.
- Patch B's changes are cohesive: fix the helper, make it non-null, and update its callers.

title: Pop foreign elements before processing HTML breakout tags
issue_md:
The HTML parser reprocesses foreign-content breakout tags as HTML, but does not first pop the foreign elements from the stack of open elements as required by the HTML specification. For example: ```java Document doc = Jsoup.parse("

One

"); System.out.println(doc.body().html()); ``` jsoup currently leaves the HTML `` inside `

One

 ``` Browsers close the foreign content before processing ``: ```html

One

 ``` Need to update the foreign-content breakout handling to pop elements until reaching a MathML text integration point, an HTML integration point, or an element in the HTML namespace before reprocessing the token. Spec: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/parsing.html#parsing-main-inforeign

title: XML doctype system IDs can serialize as invalid XML

judge.reasoning: Both patches fix the root cause the same way: when the system identifier contains a double quote, they delimit it with single quotes and leave the value unchanged. This matches the fix the issue asks for, and neither patch alters the stored identifier. Patch A applies the change only to the system ID, which is exactly the scope of the issue, and adds a CHANGES.md entry. Patch B moves the logic into a small `appendQuoted` helper and also applies it to the public ID. That goes beyond the ask, but it is low-risk and consistent: XML public IDs cannot legally contain `"`, so it only affects input from the HTML parser or programmatic construction, where it prevents the same malformed output. It is neutral rather than harmful. The deciding difference is the tests. Patch A has one test with two round-trip assertions, which is enough to fail before the fix and pass after it. Patch B's tests are more substantive. They reproduce the exact scenario from the issue, check that `systemId()` holds the unescaped value, and verify that reparsing the serialized output preserves the identifier. They also cover the HTML parser path, confirm that a single quote inside the ID still gets double quotes, and test mixed public and system IDs. Patch A's inline comment and changelog entry are good touches, but Patch B's helper is clearly documented and its broader, meaningful tests give more confidence the fix holds.

title: `W3CDom` drops some XML node types

judge.reasoning:
Both patches convert CDataNode to CDATASection, convert `<?...?>` nodes other than `xml` to ProcessingInstruction, and walk the document's children so comments and PIs outside the root are kept.

Patch A changes less of the existing code. Doctype creation stays where it was, at document creation. A tracks whether a node came before the doctype and moves it in front when needed, so document order holds. It resets `builder.dest = out` before each top-level traverse, which avoids changing the delicate `tail` ascend logic. PI detection uses the real `isDeclaration` flag, exposed through NodeInternals, so `<!ENTITY>` declarations are excluded reliably.

Patch B is riskier:
- It removes doctype creation from `fromJsoup` and recreates the doctype only during whole-document traversal. As a result, `fromJsoup(Element)`, which previously got the owner document's doctype, silently loses it. That is a behavioural regression outside the issue's scope.
- It widens the `tail` ascend condition from `getParentNode() instanceof Element` to `!= null`. That logic exists to handle elements emitted as text, so the change adds risk.
- It detects PIs with `outerHtml().startsWith("<?")`, which is fragile and costly compared with using the flag.
- Its CDATA fallback is harmless.

On tests, Patch A is clearly stronger. It checks the exact child sequence and count at document level, ordering around a doctype, PIs inside elements, exclusion of the XML declaration and markup declarations, the source user data link, CDATA in both XML and HTML (SVG), subtree conversion, and serialized output. Patch B's three tests are thinner and do not check full child counts or exclusion of declarations.

Patch A is the safer and better-tested fix.

issue_md:
`W3CDom.fromJsoup(...)` currently drops XML processing instructions and comments outside the root element, and converts `CDataNode` instances to ordinary text nodes.

All three have direct W3C DOM equivalents, so conversion should preserve them and their document order. XML declarations and doctype internal subsets remain out of scope.

title: XML serialization drops attributes whose names start with a digit or hyphen

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the root cause the same way. Each changes `Attribute.getValidKey` so that an XML key with an invalid first character (digit, hyphen, dot) gets a leading `_` instead of returning null. That fixes the dropped attributes in the issue (`1a` → `_1a`, `-a` → `_-a`). Because element tag names go through the same helper, both also repair invalid element names, and both simplify the W3CDom fallback paths that this change makes redundant.

The difference is correctness at an edge the fix itself creates. Once invalid names are repaired by prefixing `_`, a repaired name can collide with an existing valid one. For example, `<root 1a='one' _1a='two'>` under Patch A serializes as `_1a="one" _1a="two"`. Duplicate attributes are not well-formed XML, so the output is still broken, just in a different way. Patch B addresses this directly in `Attributes.html`:

issue_md:
Currently some parser paths use `Normalizer.normalize(...)` for names that require narrower rules.

The current implementation trims with `String.trim()` and lowercases with Unicode rules. That can remove control characters from accepted tag and attribute names, and can make non-ASCII names compare as equal to ASCII names. The HTML5 spec has tag and attribute names as ASCII case insensitive.

For example, these should not equal:

```text
"data-x\u0001"
"data-x"

"K"
"k"

"ſ"
"s"
```

HTML name comparisons should use ASCII-only case folding. XML parsing should preserve exact names unless the configured parse settings request ASCII folding.

This affects tag and attribute identity, duplicate detection, selector matching, and contextual parser choices.

title: Update select parsing to the current HTML Standard
issue_md:
jsoup has the former `InSelect` and `InSelectInTable` insertion modes.

The current [HTML parsing rules](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/parsing.html#parsing-main-inbody) handle `select` content through the in-body insertion mode, including customizable select content.

We should update the tree builder to follow the current rules and retire the obsolete select insertion modes.
